summary:
Santa Cruz province stands under Argentina's national framework on gender identity, and no provincial departure from that framework material enough to score separately has been sourced. The operating position for a visitor to the province is the national one.

Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval. An 'X' marker has been available on the national identity document since 2021. The United Nations described the statute as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal. Decree DNU 62/2025, published on 5 February 2025, amended Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law to bar under-18s from gender-affirming surgical and hormonal interventions, and Reuters reported the resulting ban on surgery and hormone therapy for adolescents. DNU 61/2025 altered the prison-sentencing law to change the placement of trans detainees. Both decrees apply nationally, to every province including Santa Cruz.

Legal experts and LGBTIQ+ organisations called both decrees unconstitutional, stated that abruptly suspending adolescent treatments endangers trans youth, and petitioned the courts to intervene. The outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a rate of one every 38 hours, figures Agencia Presentes published on 19 March 2026 alongside a description of the year as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeal court had removed in 2020. The gender-motivated aggravator is therefore not applied in that case as it now stands.

Trans activists interviewed in April 2025 said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate, reporting that the 2012 law remains formally in force but is no longer guaranteed in practice.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws. An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 nonetheless records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration across the legal and civic environment rather than in any single statute.

The national Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry was eliminated under President Milei, removing the federal body that had coordinated policy for the community. Activists told the Washington Blade on 10 April 2025 that this, together with the February 2025 decrees, has produced a chaotic and desperate situation for transgender Argentines.

The 2012 statute's standing as one of the most permissive legal gender recognition regimes in the world is a point of comparison that no longer describes the operating reality on its own: the law has not been repealed, but executive decrees and the reported non-enforcement of protections have narrowed what it delivers in practice.
localsOnly:
The federal Trans Labor Quota Law reserves 1% of public-sector posts for trans workers. Activists reported in April 2025 that the Milei government dismissed trans hires made under the quota and that the measure is no longer being implemented, leaving residents who depend on public employment without the statutory preference.

DNU 61/2025 governs the housing of transgender people in prison, a measure that falls on residents in the provincial prison system rather than on visitors. Legal experts and LGBTIQ+ organisations challenged it alongside the decree on minors, on the ground that both were adopted without the required legislative process.

Anti-discrimination protections available to residents run through national law and through the laws of individual provinces; the sources do not record a Santa Cruz provincial anti-discrimination instrument by name.
outOfScopeNotes:
The constitutional challenge to DNU 62/2025 and DNU 61/2025 was filed but its outcome is unresolved in the sources available here. No court ruling on the decrees' validity is recorded, so their current binding status should be treated as unresolved rather than settled.

No Santa Cruz-specific material was sourced for this record. Provincial police practice, the availability of identity document services in the province, provincial hate-crime figures, and any provincial-level policy on gender identity are not covered and remain unverified.

Whether the Trans Labor Quota Law's non-implementation reflects a formal suspension, a change of regulation, or non-enforcement at agency level is not sourced; only activists' testimony that it is no longer being applied is on record.

The Outright International assessments of 12 March 2026 are national-level ratings, and the specific provincial or legal criteria behind each negative rating are not set out in the material available here.
